articles.title: Bryson DeChambeau speaks out for first time since LIV Golf shutdown, reveals immediate plans for December
articles.summary: In his first public statement since LIV Golf announced its shutdown, Bryson DeChambeau reflects on his time with the league and discusses his upcoming participation in the Nedbank Golf Challenge in December, while leaving his long-term plans open-ended amid critical deadlines for joining established tours.
articles.body: Bryson DeChambeau has spoken publicly for the first time since LIV Golf confirmed it would wind down operations, reflecting on his four years with the Saudi-backed league while leaving his own future unresolved. The two-time US Open champion stopped short of confirming whether he intends to return to the PGA Tour or join the DP World Tour, with a key membership deadline approaching.DeChambeau reflects on four years with LIV GolfDeChambeau joined LIV Golf in 2022, becoming one of the most prominent players to leave the established professional circuit for the breakaway league. His decision came during a period of significant upheaval in men's golf, when players including Brooks Koepka, Dustin Johnson and Phil Mickelson also accepted reported eight- and nine-figure contracts to join the Saudi-backed competition.The defections triggered a prolonged dispute between LIV Golf and the established tours. The PGA Tour and European Tour initially imposed restrictions on players who had joined the breakaway circuit, although some of those rules have since been relaxed.Following LIV Golf's announcement that it would cease operations, DeChambeau issued a statement reflecting on his time with the league without expressing regret over his decision.“I’m not going to rewrite the past four years,” he said.“I made a decision I believed in, and I’m grateful for what came with it: playing in front of fans new and old around the world who rarely got to see the best players at home.”He singled out Adelaide in Australia and Johannesburg in South Africa among the destinations that made a lasting impression during his time with LIV Golf.The American also defended the league's team format, which he believes remains a worthwhile concept even if its future structure changes. LIV Golf's tournaments featured 57 players divided into 13 teams, with separate individual and team competitions, before the season concluded with a bracket-style team championship involving singles and alternate-shot matches.“I still believe in team golf,” DeChambeau said. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.”He added that he had given everything he could to make the format work during his time with the league.What happens next for DeChambeau?While DeChambeau made clear that his commitment to growing the sport remains unchanged, he offered no confirmation about where he intends to compete once LIV Golf shuts down.His immediate schedule includes the Nedbank Golf Challenge in December, Gary Player's tournament in South Africa. DeChambeau said he was looking forward to returning after the reception he received during his first visit to the country.“In December, I’ll compete at the Nedbank Golf Challenge, Gary Player’s event, in front of fans who made my first visit to South Africa unforgettable. Beyond that, I’ll go about whatever is next the right way,” he said.“My passion is to grow this game. That’s still the goal. Thank you for sticking with me. Together we can grow this great game we all love.”The question of his longer-term future remains significant because DeChambeau has until November 15 to declare his intention to become a member of the DP World Tour. Missing that deadline could leave him without a straightforward route back into the established professional circuits, potentially limiting his opportunities beyond the major championships.DeChambeau is among the most recognisable figures in modern golf, with nine PGA Tour victories and two US Open titles. He won his first major at Winged Foot in 2020 before claiming a second at Pinehurst in 2024.LIV Golf's shutdown followed the withdrawal of financial backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The league had been unable to secure the additional investment required to proceed with its proposed LIV 2.0 plans for 2027, and confirmed in US bankruptcy court on Thursday that it would wind down operations.For DeChambeau, the immediate commitment is South Africa. What follows will depend on the decisions he makes as the breakaway league's players begin considering their next steps.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Welcome to college football's new reality: Make the 24-team playoff or get fired
articles.summary: Will more playoff access really calm down the "Fire Everyone" culture in college football? Here's a prediction: It'll make it far, far worse.
articles.body:
As support grew for the College Football Playoff to expand from 12 to 24 teams, money was not the primary factor.

Yes, the new five-year, $1.7 billion deal finalized Monday will add a few million for each school in the SEC and Big Ten and a smaller amount for everyone else. But replacing conference championship games with a bunch of first-round playoff games was not, on its own, a big enough pot of gold to blow up the entire sport and risk losing the sanctity of the regular season.

What was worth it? Access. As coaches and administrators experienced the 12-team playoff, they came to the conclusion — and probably correctly — that nothing resonates with fans anymore besides getting into the field. They increasingly saw their own job security tied to the black-and-white standard of being in or out, so they simply changed the standard to include far more programs stuck in the middle of the two richest conferences.

But will more playoff access really calm down the "Fire Everyone" culture that seems to be increasingly pervasive in college football? Here's a prediction: It'll make it far, far worse.

Though it was a slow start to this year's coaching carousel, business is picking up with four power conference openings and several more that could materialize in the coming weeks. The real surprise, though, is how many first-year coaches are already under pressure.

Michigan's Kyle Whittingham, California's Tosh Lupoi, Washington State's Kirby Moore, Colorado State's Jim Mora and Tulane's Will Hall have been so disappointing in Year 1 that it wouldn't be a shock if their schools pulled the plug and started over. Even at places like Arkansas and Florida, where the record is no different from what was expected, first-year coaches are struggling to convince fans they are on the right track.

Traditionally, firing a coach after one year was taboo unless there was an off-field scandal. Even if it was immediately clear to university administrators that they hired a coach who was in over his head, it was almost too embarrassing to admit such a mistake without at least two years of on-field evidence.

But if that culture is indeed changing and compressing the timeline for coaches to prove themselves, the 24-team playoff is going to be like dumping kerosene on a bonfire.

If you thought the 12-team playoff created a world of FOMO for everyone who didn't get in, just wait until two-thirds of the power conference schools realize every November that they landed on the wrong side of a pass-fail test.

When the standard is really, really high to make the playoff, you can at least rationalize not making it. Even now, in the 12-team version, we have seen good teams like Texas, Notre Dame and Vanderbilt last year all fall short because there wasn't enough room and the margin for error was small. If you fell short of the cut line, you were in good company.

So when you change the threshold so dramatically, you are of course including more teams worthy of a shot. But you are also creating a new standard for what constitutes a successful season. It's inevitable that, starting next year, fans and boosters will consume college football in a much more binary fashion: You're either in or you're out, and it's a big problem if you're out.

At the same time, college football is undergoing an Overton window revolution on what kind of season is acceptable for a new coach. It used to be, the first year was a free pass. Especially at programs that had lost for a few years, the results didn't matter. All you had to do was show that you've changed the locker room culture, be a little bit more competitive than the last coach, and secure a good recruiting class to keep fans happy.

Those days are gone. Even if Curt Cignetti getting Indiana to the playoff in Year 1 and winning a national title in Year 2 is the extreme example, he's far from alone in using the transfer portal to engineer an immediate turnaround. When fans see Bob Chesney get UCLA to 9-0, Will Stein put Kentucky into the CFP mix, Eric Morris win quickly at Oklahoma State with players he coached at North Texas and James Franklin put the best Virginia Tech team on the field in nearly a decade, everyone has a right to ask, "Why not us?"

If you're trying to figure out what's fueling so much anger right now at a place like Florida, which is 5-4 and has not been bad overall in Jon Sumrall's first year, look no further. Under a traditional timeline, Florida fans would generally be in agreement that Sumrall needs time to rebuild the program after five straight mediocre (or worse) seasons and wouldn't start rendering any judgments until Year 3.

But now that it's proven you can flip any program in a year, that becomes the expectation. Nobody can afford to play the long game anymore. At 5-4 with wins over Texas and Ole Miss, Sumrall is not on the hot seat and has largely been fine. But will the chatter about his job security move from the online world to the real world if he's not on track to make the 24-team playoff at this time next year?

The collision of those two factors — expanding the playoff and the recent track record of coaches winning in Year 1 — will inevitably accelerate all the conversations fans are having when they start to wonder if they've got the right guy. And as we see around the country every year, prohibitive finances are no match for administrative self-preservation.

For weeks, Florida State officials were adamant that they wanted to bring back Mike Norvell, largely because his approximate $50 million buyout was such an issue. When the noise got loud enough, though, the school president caved. We could see the same thing starting to unfold at Nebraska, where Matt Rhule signed a new contract last year with a $63 million buyout but now finds himself at the center of a fan mutiny after losing four straight.

These are not healthy developments, but Newton's Third Law of Motion always wins in the end. For every action (massive coaching contracts, playoff expansion, transfer portal free-for-all), there will be an equal and opposite reaction (new expectations, more pressure, less patience to build from the ground up). The old rules no longer apply.

But there is a real problem with what they've done here. At 24 teams, there are still going to be more losers than winners at the end of every college football season; only now, it will make the line between the two that much brighter. Everyone will feel that much more pressure to be on the right side of the divide because it will be viewed as unacceptable to fall short.

There are plenty of reasons why expanding the playoff makes sense. Increased parity means more than 12 teams deserve a chance, donors are being asked to pour $40-50 million into rosters without enough postseason rewards and there was no way to rescue the bowl system given all the focus on the CFP. The conference championship games had also gotten stale since realignment helped form 16- and 18-team mega-conferences, so there is some logic in replacing them with first-round playoff games.

But if coaches and administrators think that a team squeaking into the playoff as the No. 22 seed will spare them from the "Fire Everyone" culture they seek to tame, it will prove to be a delusion. And if God forbid they miss the 24-team playoff, they will soon get a lesson in unintended consequences.

articles.title: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino reportedly among top candidates to join Manchester United if Michael Carrick is fired
articles.summary: Pochettino signed an extension this summer to stay with the U.S. through the 2030 World Cup, but that contract reportedly includes a $10 million release clau...
articles.body:
With Manchester United in dire straits, the English club might be looking to United States men's national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino as a potential new leader. Pochettino has emerged as one of the favored candidates to succeed United manager Michael Carrick if he is fired, ESPN reported Monday .

United is currently third-to-last in the Premier League table and facing relegation for the first time since the division was created. Carrick has spent the season on the hot seat, but is on the brink of finally being sacked after failing to turn the season around.

ESPN reports that discussions on whether to fire Carrick are still ongoing, but there is a sense of "acceptance" that a new manager is needed.

Candidates that are reportedly being considered include former Newcastle coach Eddie Howe, former Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann and former Ipswich Town head coach Kieran McKenna, per ESPN. But Pochettino, who coached at Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea before taking the USMNT job in 2024, has reportedly emerged as a frontrunner.

Pochettino agreed to stay with the USMNT on a new contract in early August, with the deal keeping the 54-year-old Argentine in charge of the Stars and Stripes through the 2030 World Cup. Coming off its best World Cup performance in decades, the move was intended to give the U.S. some continuity for the next four-year World Cup cycle.

ESPN reports that Pochettino's contract includes a $10 million release clause, which Man United would have to pay in order to hire Pochettino.

Manchester United started the 2026-27 Premier League season with a stunning 2-0 loss to recently promoted Hull City. Things have not gotten much better for the team since then, with highlights including a derby loss to a short-handed Manchester City and a crumbling 2-0 loss to Chelsea last week.

The Red Devils currently have only one win across the first 10 games of the season, and are one point out of last place in the Premier League.

Pochettino has expressed an interest in embracing a "fresh start" for the next cycle, and has utilized the country's young up-and-coming players in recent international breaks. However, Pochettino's departure would leave the USMNT without that sense of direction, though with plenty of time to find a new coach before the next World Cup.

articles.title: Bayern Munich midfielder Aleksandar Pavlović ‘delighted’ for Lennart Karl’s redemption
articles.summary: FC Bayern’s starlet is hustling and bustling to prove a point
articles.body:
Lennart Karl started the season in terrible form and was in the crosshairs of every single Bayern Munich fan, but the 18-year-old appears to have turned a corner with decent performances against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League and now a hard-fought 2-1 win against Mainz.

"I think, as a professional footballer, you simply have to be able to deal with things like that," Karl's teammate Aleksandar Pavlović said after the Mainz game (via @iMiaSanMia ). "I don't think he pays too much attention to what's going on outside. He just gets on with things and plays his football. I'm obviously delighted that he scored today as well."

Despite being undefeated this season so far, Bayern has not been playing at its highest level. This is a time when the team must rally together and put in a shift to get results. For Karl, he's done exactly that and wants to remind us why he was the breakout star of last season for Bayern.

articles.title: Everything Dan Lanning said before Oregon hosts Michigan
articles.summary: Dan Lanning looked back at Oregon's win over Ohio State and previewed the Ducks' matchup vs. Michigan at his weekly press conference.
articles.body:
The Oregon Ducks are riding high off back-to-back wins over ranked opponents and are suddenly back in the hunt for spots in both the Big Ten title game and the College Football Playoff. However, the Ducks will need to avoid a letdown at home this week against the Michigan Wolverines .

Dan Lanning has the Oregon offense rolling with Jay Johnson as the play-caller, and Dylan Raiola's steady play and downfield aggressiveness have given the Ducks a chance to finish the season strong and sneak into the playoff field. A 41-28 victory on the road over Ohio State was the last major hurdle for the Ducks to clear, but the Wolverines have made changes this week in anticipation of a trip to Eugene.

Coming off a 15-6 loss at home to Michigan State, Michigan fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck and reopened the quarterback competition in Ann Arbor between Bryce Underwood and Tommy Carr. The Wolverines' offense has been inept all season long, but some changes this week could make it a challenge to prepare for.

Oregon and Michigan have both played well defensively in recent weeks, meaning possessions and points could be at a premium on Saturday at Autzen Stadium. At his weekly press conference on Monday night, Lanning looked back on the win at Ohio State, addressed key injuries the Ducks are dealing with, and previewed this weekend's matchup with the Wolverines. Here is everything Lanning had to say before the Ducks host Michigan:

Dan Lanning: "Fun game there in Columbus. Obviously had some ebbs and flows, but really got on a heater with our players and, I think, saw some of the things we're capable of doing as a team. Just challenged our team that I want to see that team continue to grow, but there were some versions of us that were the best versions of us on Saturday. Fun thing to be a part of. Our guys came back and attacked at work today. (We are) about to play a Michigan team that's had some struggles, but you also see some unbelievable personnel. We've had the opportunity to go against coach Whittingham before and see where they really show up. They've always been tough-nosed. You see physicality. Obviously, their defense is probably as good as any defense that we played this season. They're playing really, really well. They've done some good things on special teams, and yes, they've had some struggles on offense, obviously, and recently had the coordinator change, but you do see a lot of talent over there. You see some talent on the offensive line. You see skill positions that can do things, and you see some quarterbacks that present different challenges. So this will be a fun prep week for us, a great opportunity to get our fans back in Autzen Stadium and get to experience that atmosphere and let them know what playing at Autzen is all about. We haven't had Michigan here at Autzen since we joined the Big Ten, so this will be a fun experience for us, especially with the rivalries and the opportunities that get created by being in this conference. So excited for it, and our guys are prepping hard to go to work."

Question: "You kind of alluded to it, some stretches in that game where you really looked like a great version of yourselves. Also a couple of potential turnovers they might have come up with that could have swung things. How do you feel like guys have balanced the last couple days, appreciating that you continue to show some growth the last couple weeks, while also knowing there's still more to be had?"

DL: "Yeah, I think it's just that you're really open and honest and point out exactly the reality of, 'OK, this went really well. Why did it go really well? This didn't go well.' There were plays that were called multiple times in the game; one time it's a touchdown, one time it's a tackle for loss on offense. Same thing with defenses that are called in the game, but I really do feel like a lot of our mindset going into that game was just do your job. When our guys went out there and did their job, they did it at a really high level and looked as good as any team in the country."

Q: "You guys were really good on third-and-long in this game. Conversely, you struggled on first down, especially running the ball. Is that scheme? Is it execution? What can you do better to not get behind the chains so much on first down?"

DL: "Yeah, I think that's something for us to certainly look at and attack. Again, some of those moments were the same play call, and it worked on one down and didn't work on the other. That usually goes back to some execution or a little bit different looks here and there. We've got to be better in some of those moments, and some of the play style and what we were trying to do. Ohio State has a really good defense as well. So I think our answers on third down — we spent a lot of time on third-and-long this past week with our offense, and we were able to take advantage of it because of that time that we put in."

Q: "Want to ask you about the touchdown right before half and why that was the right moment for that particular look, and then also Jamari as a ball carrier. Why was that a good fit?"

DL: "Obviously we've done some of the gate stuff in the past. That's a play that we've worked with our field goal unit since fall camp, and we knew we were going to utilize it as a gate play, so we put that in with our offense several weeks ago, and felt like that was a play that was going to be successful. It had a couple different options. You also have the ability to burn the timeout if you don't like the look right there, and you can take points. But we liked the look that we saw. He had taken snaps and done that QB sneak 50 times, at least, since August. Not necessarily with that exact same formation or the exact same personnel on the field, but several times the last few weeks, and our history against Ohio State, we've run gate against them multiple times, so we anticipated them trying to defend some of those different looks that we give them. We'd run outside runs. We'd done some different looks, but we hadn't done that, so we felt like there was a great chance it was going to be there and be available. When we saw the look, we knew it was going to be positive, and that's kind of our game on the line play from the 2-yard line and the 1-yard line, and it fit. It felt like that was a great time to take that chance and that opportunity."

Q: "The worry Saturday was if it was something serious for Teitum. Do you have an update there, and what can you say about what he means to the program?"

DL: "Teitum has been unbelievable for us this year, and every year that he's been here. Just watching him grow as a player and a person has been a lot of fun for us. But unfortunately, Teitum's done for the year. He had a knee injury. He'll end up having surgery. He's gonna have to wait for a little bit to let things settle down. I hate it for him, because it's kind of a routine, weird play that it happened on. He obviously was a huge impact in that game. You look at the fake punt and the impact that he's had on our team throughout the year. Normally I'd wait till Wednesday to talk about that, but probably not fair to him. So we'll see him walking around on crutches, and he left it on the line there on the field, man. I don't know if he'll get another chance to play as an Oregon football player, but whoever gets to have that guy on their team in the future is going to be really, really lucky."

Q: "You mentioned the struggles that Michigan is going through offensively. I feel like a lot of teams have dealt with some challenges, especially on the offensive side. You mentioned post-game where you guys were just two weeks ago, and the changes that you guys have made, the growth that you've made. I feel like those challenges for teams have created more parity across the board. What do you attribute the parity in college football to this season?"

DL: "I'm not sure what you're saying. Are you saying the coordinator changes have created the parity or what?"

Q: "I'm asking what you can attribute to the parity, because I feel like we always talk about how the college football season has a lot of parity in it, but I feel like this season we've seen more parity than usual. I'm curious if you have that same perspective and what you attribute the parity to."

DL: "I mean, 10 years ago, some of the best teams in college football had great players stacked, and there wasn't the opportunity for those players necessarily to go somewhere else. Now I think with NIL and some of the things that happen with the portal, there are a lot of transactions that happen each season, and guys that are good players aren't necessarily stacked in depth behind other good players on rosters. That's hard. We're fortunate to have a really good roster here, but there's transition every year, and I think what you see is more guys that would have been a really good two here, now they go somewhere else and they become a one, and then they develop and grow as a player, and they become really good players. I think that part of it is the distribution of talent is higher now than it's ever been. I think that's definitely one piece of the parity. The reality of playing in the conference that we're in is it looks a lot different than it did five years ago, 10 years ago. This is a really challenging conference. There are other challenging conferences in college football; they're big, and every week it's a talented team that you're playing against that has good coaches, and they have good players, and that makes it a real challenge."

Q: "You guys have had to prep for multiple quarterbacks before, but what makes (Michigan's) two quarterbacks different?"

DL: "Yeah, there are some things that are similar, and then some things that are different. Obviously, more recently, I think if you look at it, it's about who's protecting the ball better. Bryce, the strength of his arm and as a running threat is unique, but they both operate similarly. The offense (doesn't) completely change based on which guy's in the game, right? There's still some similarities in what they do now. Will it change now moving forward? That's where we have to go back and evaluate some of our Utah games. Coach Harding's been with coach Whittingham for a long, long time, so I think there's going to be some high-identity plays that probably show up based on what he's done in his history. You've got to evaluate our games. They also have a coach on staff there that's going to have some involvement, that's been at Syracuse, so you go back and look at that. But when you look at the quarterbacks, there's some similar pieces to what they both do. Just some small variances and differences."

Q: "J-Mac played a little bit in this game. What have you seen from him more as a person than as a player over these past two weeks as he's battled back from the injury and tried to get back to the player he was before going down?"

DL: "Yeah, I mean, just unbelievable resilience to return as fast as he could. It's always hard to level expectations because he wanted more than anything to be in as much as he could. He worked really, really hard to put himself in a position to get back, but I knew early in the week, like, 'Hey man, we need you not just for one, we need you for several.' So this could be — this is a build-up process, and you don't go from not playing any football at all to going to play at a really high level for a lot of snaps. When he was in there, he did a really good job. Sometimes he's open. I wish we could have been able to find him, but I think his leadership continues to show up. His work ethic continues to show up, and obviously he's a big piece of our offense and a dynamic piece. So, excited to have him back out there."

Q: "Obviously, you don't replace someone like Teitum with one player. Nasir (Wyatt) is a name that will come up. But is there anybody else? What's the plan for working without Teitum?"

DL: "I wouldn't necessarily share everybody that's going to be involved in that, but obviously Nas will step up. He's a guy that's been out there for us already, but there will be some moving parts. It'll look a little bit different. There's already been a rotation along our defensive line, so I think you'll see a lot of the familiar faces. But you don't just replace a guy like Teitum Tuioti and his experience and what he's been able to do."

Q: "Obviously, a 24-team playoff became official today. Just your thoughts on it in this moment, and then speaking to the parity that you were talking about earlier, do you feel like that parity might make a good argument for an expanded playoff?"

DL: "Yeah, not a lot of new thoughts. I mean, I think this is something the coaches have known is coming down the wire here for a little bit, so no new thoughts really on it. I do think that it's getting closer and closer to a normal playoff model in other sports, where the challenge is — we're certainly not the same team we were when we started the season, right? We've experienced some adversity, we've seen some different players on the field, we've gone through some coaching transition, but if the goal is to be able to get teams that are capable of winning at the end, I think that it allows a team like ourselves, where you can say, 'OK, the best team could be in there potentially and have a chance to go compete.' So I think you'll see some more of that. We saw it last year with Miami; they experienced a couple of losses, and they started playing their best football toward the end of the season and got all the way to the national championship. So it's gonna provide some unique opportunities. The questions about who's in, who's not in, that's just gonna exist now at a higher level of who's 20, who's 25, who's 26, who's 27. Every time the mark moves, that's always the conversation, and that'll happen again. But certainly there'll be some really quality teams playing, and obviously the loss of the conference championship games is going to be unique and sad in some respects because that's always a really awesome game to be a part of. But in reality, it's almost a punishment for those teams that are playing in it because they're playing football when nobody else is. So it certainly makes sense with the landscape of college football and what it's like right now."

Q: "Before Kyle got to Michigan, there was a lot going on in that program. You said that you've known him for a few years, gone against him before. How have you seen him handle everything that's going on this year and the ups and downs of this year and help that program get back to level ground?"

DL: "I haven't really been able to pay much attention to him until this week. So, I don't know. I know he's a Hall of Fame coach for a reason, and he's won a lot of football games. I've been worried about my own problems, not really paying attention to his. I know he does a great job. I'm sure they'll be prepared to play us."

Q: "You touched on it, just the removal of the conference championship. Do you feel that this is the right move to remove conference championships?"

DL: "I think it's a necessary evil. Like I said, I like that game. I would love for it to be a part, but I don't think it's fair necessarily to the teams. We experienced it a couple years ago. We're playing a conference championship, and everybody else is able to relax on their couch, and then we go almost a month without. I think the thing that I've always said is the game should be played in sequence, very similar to the NFL playoffs or any other playoff model. So there's still a lot to college football. I think it has to get better, but I do think if you're going to expand the games to 24 teams, then that's going to be part of what is missing."

Q: "Does Michigan's change at offensive coordinator change much for how you prepare for their offense?"

DL: "Yeah, it just makes you do a little bit of a deeper dive. Like I said, when you're trying to look to say, 'OK, what else could they pull out?' I think you know one thing you recognize about changes in college football is teams that have done that, experienced that recently, they've kind of had a resurgence on offense. I mean, whether it's a coaching change, there are several programs. I showed that to our players today. Here are programs that made changes at head coach or coordinator this season, and here's what the next week looked like or the next two weeks looked like. We've seen a lot of those teams have a lot of success. Sometimes that's not just because of a change. But there's a spark that's sometimes lit when those things happen. So we anticipate seeing their absolute best, and then we're going to have to chase ghosts a little bit and look for every answer that we might be able to find based on what might be different."

Q: "Just wondering if you could speak to the offensive line development and the sort of consistency that you've seen. Obviously, the continuity is there, but this last week in particular felt like a kind of even bigger breakthrough for that group."

DL: "Yeah, we've always felt games like that one, the rushing battle is really important. The way they're able to protect the quarterback, I think that's one of the glaring differences in that game. I know there was some chunk yardage at the end of the game that was a little different because of how we were playing defense, but ultimately, I think they rushed for like 54 yards, and we were over 100, and I think that speaks to our offense. That's a really hard front to be able to run on. We were able to protect the quarterback, and again, some of that's scheme variance, and then some of it's the way we call the game. To be able to build screens off of some of their pressures, and so all those things allow the O-line to be able to shine and have a lot of success. So I think all those things come together, and then those guys having continuity playing together, building more confidence in the calls that you're making with the guy next to you, like that, that's going to create a rhythm and allow them to perform."

Q: "I'm curious because the matchup with Michigan and what they have on that front, how is that a measuring stick? We talk about the continuity, a couple good performances, but this is a really tough group right here."

DL: "Yeah, it's as good up front as we've seen, right? There's a lot of NFL players on that defense in general, but this group, they do an unbelievable job, and it's a pressure-oriented group, from a standpoint of they're going to give you a lot. They pitch a lot of different looks. (Michigan defensive coordinator Jay Hill) has done an unbelievable job there of creating some real disruption and havoc with what they do up front, and then they play tight coverage in the back end. So there's a reason that they've had so much success defensively. It'll be a real challenge for our offensive line."

Q: "Your defense has at this point the lowest rate of missed tackles in the country. To get to that point from where you guys were at Oklahoma State, what do you attribute that to?"

Q: "I'm not sure, but probably not in that range."

DL: "Get better. Growth, right? Just a lot of work, a lot of practice. Guys taking it seriously on how they have to attack and improve. And look, that's just a sample of the previous games, right? This next game's a separate indicator, so we have to tackle well again. I know all that said, I saw some missed tackles this last game for us, so we can continue to get better there."
